correctness.rationale: With rates in units of a and hub departure multiplier h=m (edge) or 1 (vertex), use transient states C=distinct leaves, A=searcher leaf/trap hub, B=opposite. The killed Poisson matrix in order C,A,B has rows (1+x,−x,−1), (−hx(m−1)/m,1+hx,0), (−h(m−1)/m,0,x+h). The right side is all ones. Absorbing jumps enter the diagonal departure rates but not the off-diagonal transition terms. Searcher-only paths while the trap waits give a positive capture probability within fixed time uniformly in the finitely many states for each fixed parameter, establishing finiteness and uniqueness. Cramer's rule independently yields both normalized means with positive denominator D=(1+x)(1+2mx+x²); at x=0 both give 1, also the direct leaf-to-hub first-jump mean in original units 1/a. Subtracting 1 gives x times strictly decreasing quadratic brackets divided by D, with positive intercepts for m≥2 and roots equal to the two stated thresholds. Subtracting the two means gives (m−1)x(m−2−x)/D, so the positive crossover exists only for m>2, and for m=2 the edge mean is strictly lower at x>0. Independent symbolic expansion shows that each derivative numerator has positive constant term and strictly negative coefficients of all positive powers for m≥2. Hence each has a unique positive zero and gives the unique global maximum. Positive-polynomial gap identities give the uniform bounds (m+1)/2 and 2; evaluating both at x=m^(−1/2) proves the sharp limits by squeezing. The two positive-root scalings also check exactly. Replay: python3 /workspace/branches/independent_star.py (SymPy), output independent_star.out alongside. The proof covers real a>0 and b≥0, not just the finite rational samples in the frozen package. It is only for independent exponential walkers on a finite star and the specified initial leaf–hub pair, and only for the mean.

value.rationale: A star isolates degree dependence while holding the leaf rate fixed. The two standard normalizations give the same static benchmark and both have a slowdown interval, yet changing how the hub departs changes the largest delay from order m with sharp coefficient 1/2 to a uniform ceiling 2, attained in the large-degree limit. The crossover thresholds and maxima quantify a useful normalization-sensitive distinction for two-particle encounter models, beyond a few numerical comparisons or a textbook first-step calculation.
